rationale: This sample is a single tight floating-point loop (flops-4) with a tiny text section (~700 bytes, 2 functions), so virtually all execution time sits in one hot arithmetic loop where control-flow transforms are re-executed every iteration; therefore BCF and FLA get very low RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights (0.10-0.20) to keep the compiler from applying them aggressively despite their nominal security value, while their CorrectnessRisk stays moderate (0.3-0.5) since bogus-flow predicates and a flattened dispatcher rarely break pure FP code but must not be encouraged here. SUB is given the highest cost-side tolerance (RuntimeCost 0.4, SizeCost 0.3) because arithmetic substitution is cheap, size-light, and the loop contains abundant integer-convertible subexpressions, making it the best resistance-per-overhead trade for a benchmark-style kernel; IBR and ICALL get intermediate weights so they may fire selectively where the dispatcher's per-function features favor them, but their CorrectnessRisk weights (0.5-0.6) prevent blind application in a hot loop where indirect branches and calls are re-taken constantly. IGV carries the highest cost-side weights (RuntimeCost 0.6, SizeCost 0.55, CorrectnessRisk 0.65) because global-variable indirection offers little benefit in a program with almost no globals and the highest risk of breaking FP constant propagation. SPLIT is enabled with balanced weights (SecurityGain 0.5, DiversityGain 0.6, CorrectnessRisk 0.7) as a low-risk enabler that increases basic-block granularity so any applied SUB/IBR transformations have more sites to diversify, without itself adding meaningful per-iteration cost.
